Discover These 8 New Hampshire Cities That Have the Cutest Downtowns

Sarah SullivanPublished: September 29, 2026
  • Share on Facebook
  • Share on Twitter
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:24
Instaread

I have been all over New Hampshire and I've been to darn near every cute corner of the state. Sometimes, if my husband has a gig at an area venue, (he's a musician) I will go wandering while he's working.  Don't get me wrong, sometimes I stay and sit at the bar and have a cocktail and an appetizer, but if it's a beautiful day, I'd rather be outside.

David plays all over New Hampshire, so, here are my top picks for the cutest downtowns that I could spend hours exploring.

Portsmouth

Believe it or not, Portsmouth downtown used to be a lot smaller than it is now.  It's grown by leaps and bounds.  Portsmouth is now a destination for locals and tourists alike.  My favorite downtown stop:  The Friendly Toast on Congress Street.  Jimmy's Jazz & Blues Club, the Music Hall and The Goat are just a few of the must stop places to go in Portsmouth.

 

Nashua

My hometown of Nashua has made huge improvements to the downtown area since I lived there as a kid.  They now have the Nashua Center for the Arts on Main Street and one of my favorite restaurants, Surf.

Plymouth

Admittedly, I haven't been to Plymouth as much as I would like.  The downtown area refects another NH college town filled with really cool stores, coffee shops and restaurants.  There's one, in particular, that is just the best.  New Berry's on the Common, (formerly JJ Newbury Store) is a favorite.  You can get great food, part of the Common Man family of restaurants and shop for unique gifts.

Wolfeboro

The Oldest Resort town in New Hampshire, Wolfeboro, is located in the Lakes Region.  It's downtown is home to the famous Yum Yum shop, Garwoods Restaurant right on the water and Kalled Gallery, home of the most incredible, hand made, expensive jewelry.  Not that I can afford it, but it sure is puuurty to look at.

Concord

Concord, NH is home to Gibson's on Main Street. I do love a great bookstore and Gibson's is one of the best.  It's huge and has a cafe.  I could spend hours and hours here.

Dover

Downtown Dover has my heart.  I work in Dover every day, so I've seen it go through a transition or two and it's still happening.  Harvey's bakery was in Downtown Dover for over 90 years, but Dover is getting another bakery in it's same space, Aubrey's on Central, which promises to keep the old Harvey's vibe and bring new delicious food of her own.

Exeter

I love downtown Exeter.  It has a lovely bandstand in the center of the town, which admittedly, is a challenge to navigate in a car when it gets busy, but the charm of Exeter just does not quit.  From the downtown restaurants to Water Street books to the UFO Festival,  Exeter is one of my favorite downtowns to hang out in.

READ THIS:  7 Things You Need to Know About NH Before You Move Here

Keene

How could I not include Keene, NH's downtown?  I went to Keene State College and spent a lot of time downtown.  It has shops, great restaurants including Athen's Pizza that is still open after all these years and Keene used to be home to the biggest pumpkin festival that I've ever seen.  I think they've scaled things down a bit, but they still have a cool event every October.

There are other downtowns that I like too, I just don't spend as much time there.  Places like Hanover, Littletown and North Conway have that NH charm too.

What place did I miss?

15 Wild Things You Probably Didn't Know About 400-Year-Old Salem

Salem, Massachusetts is celebrating 400 years in 2026, but there's a lot more to the Witch City's story than witches and Halloween. Here are 15 surprising things you may not know about Salem's history.

Gallery Credit: Garret Doll

Credit: Getty Images

Salem Was Founded in 1626

Roger Conant moved his settlement from Cape Ann to Naumkeag in the fall of 1626, establishing the English settlement that eventually became Salem.

Salem Wasn't Originally Called Salem

Salem Wasn't Originally Called Salem

Before European colonization, the area was known as Naumkeag, often translated as "fishing place."

Credit: Getty Images

Salem's Name Is Connected to the Word "Peace"

According to Salem's official 400th-anniversary history, tradition holds that after Roger Conant peacefully turned leadership of the settlement over to John Endicott, the community became known as Salem.
The name is connected to the Hebrew word shalom, meaning peace.

The National Guard Traces Its Beginnings to Salem

The National Guard Traces Its Beginnings to Salem

In December 1636, the East Regiment of the Massachusetts Bay Colony militia was organized in Salem. The U.S. National Guard considers that organization of colonial militia units, including the one associated with Salem, part of its origin story.

Credit: Getty Images

The House of the Seven Gables Is REALLY Old

Construction of what became known as The House of the Seven Gables dates back to 1668. It eventually became famous because of Salem-born author Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1851 novel The House of the Seven Gables.


Credit: Getty Images

The Witch Trials Didn't Actually Start in What We Know as Downtown Salem

The first accusations associated with the Salem Witch Trials began in Salem Village, which is largely present-day Danvers. At the time, Salem covered a much larger geographic area than the modern city does today.

Credit: Getty Images

Twenty-Five Innocent People Died During the Witch Trials Crisis

The witch trials weren't the campy Halloween story they've sometimes become in pop culture. The events of 1692 and 1693 led to the deaths of 25 innocent women, men and children.

Credit: Getty Images

You Can Still See Real Objects Connected to the Witch Trials

The Peabody Essex Museum has authentic objects connected to the Salem Witch Trials, including court-related materials and personal objects belonging to people involved in the events.

Credit: Getty Images

Salem Became One of America's Most Important Ports

Long before Salem became known around the world for witches, it was known for ships. By the late 1700s and early 1800s, Salem merchants were involved in global trade, helping turn the city into one of America's important maritime centers.

Credit: Getty Images

One of America's First Luxury Yachts Was Built in Salem

Apparently wealthy people wanting ridiculous boats isn't exactly a new thing.
In 1816, Salem's George Crowninshield Jr. commissioned the construction of Cleopatra's Barge, described by Salem 400+ as America's first luxury yacht.


Credit: Photographer Unknown (Public Domain)

Salem Has an Incredible Connection to the Abolitionist Movement

Sarah Parker Remond was born in Salem in 1826 and became an important abolitionist. While still young, she became an agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society and eventually spoke against slavery in both the United States and Great Britain.

Credit: Getty Images

Salem Didn't Officially Become a City Until 1836

Salem dates its founding to 1626, but it remained a town for more than two centuries. It wasn't officially chartered as a city until 1836, becoming only the second Massachusetts community to receive that designation.

Credit: Getty Images

Nathaniel Hawthorne Was Actually From Salem

Salem didn't just inspire Nathaniel Hawthorne. He was born there. And his family had a direct connection to the witch trials. Hawthorne was a descendant of John Hathorne, one of the judges involved in the 1692 proceedings.

Credit: Salem Ma Firefighters Local 172 via Facebook

Salem Fire 001 - 1

Credit: Getty Images

There's a Reason They're Calling It Salem 400+

Salem could have simply thrown itself a giant 400th birthday party.
Instead, the official commemoration is called Salem 400+. That "+" is there to recognize the Indigenous history that predates the European settlement of 1626 while also looking toward what Salem becomes next.

9 NH Places Locals Recommend For Locally Sourced Meat

Gallery Credit: Katie Killourhy

Brandmoore Farm via Facebook

Brandmoore Farm in Rollinsford, NH

This Rollinsford farm was also recommended by multiple locals. According to their website, "The entire farm is approximately 400 acres, including the forested areas. We raise cows, pigs, chickens, and grow 2 acres of organic vegetables. We are proud to offer fresh milk from the farm, from our herd of Jersey cows. On the farm, we process the organic milk in our Cheesery and turn the whole, organic milk into yogurt and cheese with attention to flavor, consistency and quality."

Brandmoore Farm via Facebook

Brandmoore Farm in Rollinsford, NH

Brandmoore Farm is located at 70 Sligo Rd, Rollinsford, NH
